query: Consider the following context: Temper embrittlement, characterized by a dramatic loss of ductility within a narrow temperature window, is ubiquitous in conventional alloys but is not reported in compositionally complex or high‐entropy alloy systems. In that context, which material can be used for ductile–brittle–ductile transition, and why?

generation.hypothesis: High-entropy alloys can be used for ductile–brittle–ductile transition due to their resistance to temper embrittlement.
generation.material_initial_state: Face-centered cubic (FCC) high-entropy alloy (HEA) in a single-phase solid solution state
generation.intervention: In-situ TEM heating experiment with a heating rate of 5 K/min and a temperature range of 300 K to 1000 K
generation.conditions: Vacuum environment with a pressure of 10^-5 Pa
generation.structural_mediator: Grain boundary segregation and dislocation density
generation.mechanism: Thermally activated dislocation glide and grain boundary sliding
generation.predicted_outcome: A 30% increase in ductility compared to conventional alloys, measured by the strain-to-failure ratio, with a standard deviation of 5%
generation.baseline: Conventional alloys with a strain-to-failure ratio of 0.2
generation.boundary: Temperature range of 500 K to 800 K, where the ductile–brittle–ductile transition is expected to occur
generation.uncertainty: The exact mechanism of temper embrittlement resistance in high-entropy alloys is not fully understood, and the role of grain boundary segregation and dislocation density needs further investigation

falsification_experiment.design: In-situ TEM heating experiment with a heating rate of 5 K/min and a temperature range of 300 K to 1000 K
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the strain-to-failure ratio of the high-entropy alloy is less than 0.25, or if the grain boundary segregation and dislocation density do not change significantly with temperature, then the hypothesis is falsified

frame.system: compositionally complex or high‐entropy alloy systems and conventional alloys

families.principle: Real-time observation of microstructural changes during the ductile–brittle–ductile transition
families.best_lever: In-situ transmission electron microscopy (TEM) of high-entropy alloys

families.principle: Modeling the effects of temperature and composition on the ductile–brittle–ductile transition at the atomic scale
cues_for: compositionally complex or high‐entropy alloy systems
families.best_lever: Molecular dynamics simulations of high-entropy alloys

families.principle: Integration of experimental and simulation techniques to understand the ductile–brittle–ductile transition
families.best_lever: Combining in-situ TEM with molecular dynamics simulations of high-entropy alloys

families.principle: Systematic variation of temperature and composition to identify the ductile–brittle–ductile transition
families.best_lever: Systematic temperature variation in compositionally complex alloys
